title: Build
content:
The framework reads your attributes in a build step and turns them into a manifest (see Concepts). During development it runs that step itself on each request that needs it. You can also run it from the command line, which is useful in two situations:

To check your code. The build reports every problem it finds: a constructor parameter the container cannot fill, a REST route without permission, an invalid attribute. Running it before a commit or in CI catches mistakes without opening WordPress.

To write a release manifest. The release build uses it internally.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework build [--output=<file>]

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer build-manifest runs the same command.

Checking

Without --output, the command builds and checks the manifest and writes nothing. It builds the project whose vendor/autoload.php the Composer bin proxy loads, which is the project you run it in. Problems are listed with class and parameter names, and the exit code is 1.

The command also lists the templates of the project that override templates of the framework.

Writing a manifest

With --output, the command writes the manifest to the given file. A written manifest is a release manifest and carries the template version, which names the directory of the release's Twig cache.

Do not write generated/manifest.php into a source checkout of a theme or plugin. Its presence switches the project to release mode (see Boot and modes), and the framework stops noticing changes to your code. The release build writes it into its own copy of the project.

title: Releases and CI
content:
Releasing a theme or plugin should be a single step: push a tag. The framework provides a GitHub Actions workflow that does the rest. It builds the release ZIP, installs it into a plain WordPress, runs your browser tests against it, and attaches the ZIP to the GitHub release only if everything passed. A ZIP that fails its tests is never published.

Tags follow semantic versioning with a v prefix: v1.2.0.

Themes, child themes and plugins

Your repository calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/consumer-release.yml of the framework repository from a workflow of its own. That workflow runs on push: tags: ['v*'] and needs permissions: contents: write to attach the ZIP. The test projects theme-dev-test, theme-dev-test-child and plugin-dev-test contain working examples to copy.

Pin the workflow to a framework tag, so a new framework version never changes your release process unannounced.

The workflow:

checks out the project and wp-dev-env;

runs composer lint and npm run lint, if they are defined, and wp-app-framework build;

builds the release; when it publishes, with --expect-version set to the version of the tag, so a tag that doesn't match Version: fails;

installs the ZIP into a plain WordPress (scripts/release-test of wp-dev-env);

runs the project's browser tests (npm run test:e2e) with E2E_TARGET=release; the input e2e: false skips them.

Plugins and child themes need a theme

A theme can be tested on its own, but a plugin or a child theme needs a theme to run in. The workflow decides from the type in composer.json and the Template: header of style.css:

a plugin is installed next to the release ZIP of a theme;

a child theme is installed on top of the release ZIP of its parent theme.

The input with-theme: <owner>/<repository>@<tag> names that theme release. It is required for plugins and child themes.

Inputs

Input	Default	Purpose
repository	the calling repository	the project to release
ref	the calling ref, i.e. the tag	the revision to build
e2e	true	run the browser tests (npm run test:e2e) against the release
publish	true	attach the ZIP to the GitHub release of the tag
framework-ref	the locked version	build with another revision of the framework (the framework's release gate uses it)
wp-dev-env-ref	main	the revision of wp-dev-env that provides the tools and the release test
with-theme	–	the theme release for plugins and child themes, <owner>/<repository>@<tag>

The framework

The framework repository tests itself in two workflows:

ci.yml runs PHPUnit, Vitest and all linters on pushes and pull requests, and builds this documentation.

release.yml runs on a tag. It runs the same checks and then the release gates: theme-dev-test, plugin-dev-test and theme-dev-test-child are built with the framework of the tag (framework-ref) and tested in the browser, the plugin and the child theme with an older release of the theme, without publishing anything. Only then does it attach wp-app-framework-<version>.zip to the GitHub release – made with git archive, without the development files marked export-ignore – and publish the documentation of the tag's minor version.

The gates make sure that a framework release works for a theme, a plugin and a child theme before anyone can depend on it.

Requiring the framework

Themes and plugins require the framework from its GitHub repository by version, and the lock file pins the exact commit:

"repositories": [{"type": "vcs", "url": "https://github.com/saijsaij/wp-app-framework"}]

title: Release
content:
A framework theme or plugin cannot simply be zipped from its Git checkout. The checkout has no vendor/, the editor scripts are not built, and the dependencies are not prefixed. A site with two framework consumers would load one framework for both of them.

wp-app-framework release turns a checkout into a ZIP that runs in any plain WordPress installation, without Composer on the server. It ships all dependencies, including the framework and Twig, prefixed with the project's own namespace in vendor-prefixed/. Several consumers with different framework versions can therefore run side by side.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework release [--output=<zip>] [--expect-version=<version>] [--package-source=<package>=<directory>]...

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer release runs the same command. It recognizes a theme or a plugin by the type in its composer.json.

What the release build does

The command works on a copy in the system's temporary directory and never changes your checkout. It runs these steps:

Copy the project. It copies the files Git does not ignore (git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard), so uncommitted changes are included. generated/manifest.php must not exist in the checkout.

Install the dependencies. It runs composer install --no-dev --classmap-authoritative from the lock file, so the release contains exactly the versions you tested.

Prefix the dependencies. Strauss renames every dependency into the project's namespace and rewrites the project's own code to use the new names. Strauss must be in the PATH; the tools image of wp-dev-env provides it.
Then the command patches Twig. Twig's compiler writes class names such as use Twig\Environment; as plain strings into every compiled template, and no prefixing tool rewrites strings. Release\TwigPatcher rewrites exactly these places. It expects each pattern a fixed number of times, so a Twig update that changes them fails the build instead of producing a broken release.

Build the manifest. It builds generated/manifest.php with the prefixed classes (using bin/wp-app-framework-prefixed.php in the prefixed copy) and writes the template version into it. Then it compiles all templates of the project and the framework, as release mode would, and checks the compiled code for names that were not prefixed.

Build the assets. If there is a package.json, it runs npm ci && npm run build, which also builds the editor runtime from vendor/.

Remove development files. It removes node_modules/, vendor/, composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json and every path the project marks export-ignore in .gitattributes (use dir/** for directories). Then it checks all PHP files for names of dependencies that were not prefixed, in string literals too. Inside vendor-prefixed/ string literals are not checked, because dependencies mention their own class names in messages.

Write the ZIP. It writes dist/<slug>-<version>.zip, or the file given with --output, with the project directory as root. The slug is the directory name. The version is the Version: header of the theme's or child theme's style.css, or of the plugin's main file <slug>.php. --expect-version makes the build fail if the version differs, which CI uses to compare it with the tag.

A child theme is built without its parent theme. Calls of the parent's public template callables compile without it.

Every step fails with the file, command or setting at fault. On failure the build directory is kept, and its path is printed, so you can look at what went wrong.

Strauss settings

The project declares the Strauss settings in its composer.json. The command cannot add them itself, because extra is part of the lock file's content hash. It checks the values it relies on instead:

"extra": {
    "strauss": {
        "target_directory": "vendor-prefixed",
        "namespace_prefix": "Vendor\\Theme\\Vendor\\",
        "classmap_prefix": "Vendor_Theme_Vendor_",
        "include_root_autoload": true,
        "update_call_sites": ["src", "functions.php"],
        "delete_vendor_packages": false
    }
}

namespace_prefix and classmap_prefix name the prefix for the dependencies. The prefix must not be the project's own namespace, which is Strauss' default.

update_call_sites lists where Strauss rewrites your code to the prefixed names. It must contain the file that boots the framework: functions.php of a theme or child theme, <slug>.php of a plugin.

Leave constant_prefix unset. It would rename the constants that the Symfony polyfills define for PHP itself, such as MB_CASE_UPPER. Twig defines no constants.

Unreleased framework changes

Normally the release uses the framework version from the lock file. To test a release with framework changes that are not released yet, replace the package with a local checkout:

composer release -- --package-source=saij/wp-app-framework=../wp-app-framework

--package-source=<package>=<directory> copies the checkout's files without those marked export-ignore, like a distribution archive. The output says that the build is not from the lock file. Composer path repositories are not supported, because the temporary copy has no sibling checkouts.

title: Concepts
content:
This page explains the ideas that the rest of the documentation relies on: who uses the framework, what happens in the build and what happens at run time, and how a block travels from a PHP class to the page and to the editor. You don't need it to follow Getting started, but the guides make more sense once you know it.

Consumers and instances

The framework is a Composer library. A project that includes it is a consumer. There are three kinds:

a theme, which boots the framework with Theme::boot();

a plugin, which boots it with Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

a child theme with code of its own (blocks, hooks, REST routes), which boots it with ChildTheme::boot(). A child theme that only overrides templates and adjusts theme.json needs no framework code at all.

Every consumer that boots creates its own instance of the framework. Instances are strictly separated. Everything with a global name is derived from the consumer's slug, its directory name: the REST route of the editor, the script handles, the JavaScript global window.wpAppFramework[slug], the cache directory wp-content/cache/{slug}/, the init action wp_app_framework/init/{slug} and the option names of settings.

The separation goes further in a release. Each consumer ships its own copy of the framework and its dependencies, prefixed with its own namespace. A theme built with framework 0.6 and a plugin built with 0.7 load different classes and don't interfere with each other. The flip side is that instances cannot pass framework objects to each other. When a plugin wants to offer something to the theme, it does so through a public interface made of WordPress filters named after its slug (see Plugins).

Build and run time

You declare almost everything with PHP attributes: #[Hook] on a method registers a hook, #[RestRoute] a REST route, #[Block] a block, #[TemplateFunction] a Twig function, #[SettingsGroup] a group of settings. Nothing reads these attributes while WordPress handles a request in production. Instead, a build step reads them once and writes a manifest: plain PHP data listing the hooks, routes, blocks with their attribute schemas, template functions, settings and the services with their constructor dependencies.

This has two benefits. First, mistakes surface early. A REST route without a permission, a constructor parameter the container cannot fill, a template function with the name of a Twig built-in – each is a build error naming the class at fault, not a surprise in production. Second, a release does no extra work at run time: it loads the manifest and calls your classes, without reflection, without checking files, and without ever writing into the theme or plugin directory.

You can run the checks yourself at any time with composer build-manifest (see Build).

Development mode and release mode

You don't run the build by hand while you develop. The framework picks one of two modes:

Release mode applies when the consumer contains generated/manifest.php. Only the release build writes that file, so this is what runs on a live site.

Development mode applies otherwise, for example in your Git checkout. The framework builds the manifest itself on the first request and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/. On each request it checks whether your classes changed in a way that matters – a new attribute, a changed signature – and rebuilds only then. You edit a file and reload the page.

Boot and modes describes both modes in detail.

Services

Your classes don't create each other. Concrete classes in your PSR-4 directories are service candidates (with a few exceptions such as enums and attribute classes), and the framework's container creates them when needed, passing other services into their constructors. A class that has a hook, a REST route, a template function or filter, or a block is an entry point; everything it needs is created for it, and only when the hook fires, the route is called or the block renders. See Services.

How a block works

Blocks show how these pieces fit together. A block consists of three files next to each other:

src/Block/Teaser/
├── Teaser.php             the block: #[Block] and a render() method
├── TeaserAttributes.php   the attributes as a typed class
└── Teaser.twig            the markup

In the build, the framework reads the attribute class and derives the attribute schema from its constructor: types, defaults, the allowed values of enums, and which attributes are content. There is no block.json. On init the framework registers the block with register_block_type(), and WordPress passes the definition to the block editor by itself.

In the post content, the block is stored as a comment with its attributes as JSON:

<!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {"title":"Summer party","highlighted":true} /-->

On the front end, WordPress calls the framework when it renders the block. The framework cleans the attributes against their schema, turns them into an instance of your attribute class, and calls your block's render() method, which renders the Twig template.

In the editor, the framework's editor runtime asks the server to render the block from the same template. The template marks editable elements with field('title'). In the editor these marks become attributes on the element, and the runtime replaces the marked elements with text editors, image pickers and inner blocks. Content editors type into the real markup; there is no second template for the editor. Typing does not re-render the block, but every other change, such as a different option in the inspector, does.

TeaserAttributes.php ──build──▶ attribute schema ──▶ register_block_type()
                                                         │
             post content: <!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {…} /-->
                                                         │
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┐
     front end: render() → Teaser.twig → HTML         editor: render route → same HTML
                                                        → marked fields become editors

Blocks and Editor go into the details.

Templates in layers

Twig templates live in the src/ directory of each project, next to the code that uses them. A template name is always the full path relative to src/, such as Block/Teaser/Teaser.twig.

When the framework looks for a template, it searches several layers in order. For a theme this is the active child theme's overrides/{theme-slug}/, then the theme's src/, then the framework's src/. A file with the same path on a higher layer wins. That is how a child theme changes the markup of a theme's block without touching its code, and how a theme changes the markup of a plugin's block. See Twig templates.

Errors

The framework never hides a missing prerequisite. Missing prerequisites – a missing build output, an unknown template, a wrong boot method – raise exceptions that name the file, class or parameter at fault.

Errors in your code at run time depend on WP_DEBUG. With WP_DEBUG enabled, exceptions from hooks and blocks are rethrown, so you see them immediately. Without it, they are written to the PHP error log, and the site keeps working: a filter returns its original value, a block renders nothing. REST routes always answer with an error response instead (see REST routes).

Along the way you see every file a consumer of the framework needs and why it is there. Plugins and child themes with code of their own are set up the same way. title: Blocks
content:
Blocks are the heart of a framework theme. Every block is rendered on the server from a Twig template, and content editors edit it inline in the editor canvas. This page shows how to write a block, which attributes it can have and how its values reach the markup. How blocks are stored A WordPress block usually stores its HTML in the post content. Once saved, that HTML stays as it is: changing the block's markup later means either migrating old posts or leaving them with the old markup. Framework blocks store no markup. The post content holds only the block comment with the attributes as JSON: When the page is displayed, the framework renders the block from its Twig template. A change to the template therefore shows up in every post at once. Block supports such as alignment or an anchor are attributes as well. There is one exception: the value of a #[RichText(postContent: true)] field is stored as inline HTML without a wrapping element, e.g. Summer party. That keeps the text of paragraphs and headings in the post content, where search and other plugins expect it (see Text in the post content). Anatomy of a block A block is made of three parts: a service class with #[Block] and a render() method, a typed attribute class, and a Twig template. There is no block.json. The build derives the attribute schema from the attribute class, and WordPress passes it to the editor on its own (through get_block_editor_server_block_settings()). The schema and the PHP object you work with therefore always match. Here is a hero block with a topline, a headline, an image, a gradient and a list of buttons. The block class use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Align; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Block; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\BlockCategory; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Supports; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer; #[Block('sections/hero', title: 'Hero', category: BlockCategory::Design, icon: 'cover-image')] #[Supports(anchor: true, align: [Align::Wide, Align::Full])] final class Hero { public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $renderer) { } public function render(HeroAttributes $attrs, string $content, WP_Block $block): string { return $this->renderer->render('Block/Hero/Hero.twig', ['attrs' => $attrs, 'content' => $content]); } } #[Block] names the block and describes it for the inserter. #[Supports] switches on WordPress features: here an HTML anchor and the wide and full alignments. render() receives what it asks for. HeroAttributes is the attribute object, string $content the rendered inner blocks, and WP_Block $block WordPress' block instance. A block that asks for $content can contain inner blocks. The attribute class use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Content; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Image; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Label; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\PlainText; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\RichText; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\ListOf; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Url; final readonly class HeroAttributes { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $topline = '', #[RichText(allowedFormats: ['core/bold', 'core/italic'])] public string $headline = '', #[Image] #[Label('Image')] public ?int $imageId = null, public Gradient $gradient = Gradient::Black, #[ListOf(Button::class)] public array $buttons = [], ) { } } final readonly class Button { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $label, #[Content] #[Url] public string $url = '', ) { } } Each constructor parameter becomes an attribute, and its type decides how it is edited: $topline and $headline are edited in the canvas: plain text, and rich text with bold and italic. $imageId is an image chosen from the media library in the canvas. Only the attachment ID is stored. $gradient is a backed enum. The editor shows a select with its cases in the inspector. $buttons is a list of Button value objects. The inspector shows a list editor, and each button's label is edited in the canvas. The template
{% if attrs.topline or is_editor() %} {{ attrs.topline }}

{% endif %} {{ attrs.headline|raw }} {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, 'large') }} {% for button in attrs.buttons %} {{ button.label }} {% endfor %} {{ content|raw }}
The template is ordinary Twig with a few helpers: block_wrapper_attributes() goes on the root element. It adds the classes and the anchor of the block's supports. field('topline') marks the element that shows a field, so the editor can turn it into an editor. inner_blocks() marks where inner blocks go. is_editor() keeps the empty topline in the editor, so content editors can fill it in, while the front end leaves it out. On the front end field(), inner_blocks() and is_editor() print nothing; they only matter in the editor (see Editor). The headline is printed with |raw because it holds HTML; everything else is escaped by Twig (see Escaping). #[Block] #[Block(name, title, category, icon: '', description: '', keywords: [], usesContext: [], allowedBlocks: null, excerptWrapper: false)] goes on a service class. The name is namespace/name in lowercase letters, digits and -. The namespace belongs to the theme or plugin, for example sections/hero. The namespace core and duplicate names are build errors. The framework itself declares no blocks. The category is a BlockCategory case; an enum instead of a string lets your IDE complete it. usesContext lists the context values the block reads from WP_Block::$context. The typical case is postId in a query loop, where a block shows data of the current post. allowedBlocks limits which blocks can be inserted as inner blocks (allowed_blocks in WordPress). It requires render() to accept string $content. excerptWrapper adds a container to WordPress' excerpt_allowed_wrapper_blocks (see Excerpts). It also requires string $content. The framework registers blocks on init with api_version 3. #[Supports] #[Supports] switches on the block supports of WordPress. Its arguments and their defaults are WordPress' own: #[Supports(contentRole: false, anchor: false, align: [], customClassName: true, multiple: true, reusable: true, inserter: true, lock: true, renaming: true, customCSS: true)] Only values that differ from WordPress' defaults are registered. html is always disabled, because a framework block has no stored HTML to edit. contentRole: true is for container blocks without content of their own. WordPress 7 opens patterns and template parts in contentOnly mode, where editors may only insert blocks into containers that count as content. A block counts as content if it has a content attribute (see Fields) or contentRole: true. A section that only holds inner blocks needs contentRole: true, so that blocks can be inserted into it in contentOnly mode. customCSS, enabled by default in WordPress 7, lets users with edit_css store free CSS for each block instance. Whether to allow that is the theme's decision: per block with customCSS: false, or for all blocks with a register_block_type_args hook of its own. Settings of your own that several blocks share, such as a color scheme, are block supports of the theme or plugin, added with #[UseSupport]. render() render() is public, non-static and returns string. Its parameters are matched by type, each at most once and in any order: the attribute class, string – the rendered inner blocks, WP_Block – WordPress' block instance. Services come through the constructor. The block service is created when the block renders for the first time, not when WordPress registers it. Attribute class The attribute class is a value class (see Values). Every parameter needs a default value, because any attribute can be missing in the content: the block was inserted before the attribute existed, or the editor never set it. Some names are taken. WordPress adds the attributes lock, metadata, className, anchor, align and style itself (style comes with the customCSS support, enabled by default in WordPress 7). The attributes of the block's own block supports are taken as well. None of these can be a parameter of the attribute class. From the class, the build creates the attribute schema with type, enum, properties/items, default and role: content (see below). Fields Most blocks hold text and images that content editors should change directly where they see them. Mark these parameters, and the editor makes them editable in the canvas: #[PlainText] – inline text, on strings only. #[RichText(allowedFormats: null)] – inline HTML, on strings only. allowedFormats lists the formats the editor offers, e.g. ['core/bold']; null allows all, [] none. #[Image] – an attachment ID, on ?int only. Some values are not visible in the markup, or are better edited in a form. With inspector: true – #[RichText(inspector: true)], also on #[PlainText] and #[Image] – a field is edited in the block inspector instead of the canvas. #[Content] marks other content, such as the URL of a link. It is edited in the inspector like any other value, but it counts as content: its control appears in the inspector's "Content" group, and WordPress keeps it editable in contentOnly mode (see below). References to posts, terms and users (#[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference]) are edited with a search in the inspector, and they count as content too. Content in contentOnly mode In WordPress 7, patterns and template parts open in contentOnly mode. Content editors can change the content of blocks there, but not their design. A block without content attributes is hidden and cannot be selected. WordPress decides by the attribute's role: content. The build sets it for you: an attribute gets role: content if it, or a field nested in it, carries #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image] or #[Content], or is a reference. In the example, buttons is content because each button has a label and a URL. The marks have no effect on REST arguments. Editor labels The editor needs a label for each value. #[Label('…')] sets the label in the inspector and the placeholder of an inline field. Without it, the label is derived from the parameter name: imageId becomes "Image id". A backed enum labels its cases by implementing Block\Labeled with a method label(): string. The build evaluates it, so it may not depend on run-time state. Without it, the editor shows the case values. #[Hidden] keeps a value out of the generated inspector. It is not allowed on inline fields. Text in the post content Text blocks such as paragraphs and headings are a special case. Search, SEO plugins and exports read the raw post content, and for most blocks they find only JSON there. For a block whose whole purpose is text, it is better to keep the text in the post content. #[RichText(postContent: true)] does that. The value is stored as the block's inner HTML instead of in the block comment: inline HTML without a wrapping element. The markup around it still comes from Twig. final readonly class ParagraphAttributes { public function __construct( #[RichText(postContent: true)] public string $text = '', ) {} }

{{ attrs.text|raw }}

As the example shows, the root element of the template may be the field itself. For your code nothing changes: the template prints the value like any other. Under the hood, the attribute is a sourced attribute (source: html without selector), and the editor saves it with RawHTML. WordPress never parses sourced attributes on the server, so the framework takes the value from the block content before it creates the attribute object. The following are build errors, each for a reason: The field is not a parameter of the attribute class itself (but of a value class or a list item): only top-level values can map to the inner HTML. A block has more than one such field: there is only one inner HTML. The block has inner blocks: inner blocks and the field would share the block content. The default is not '': the editor stores an empty value as empty block content. Excerpts WordPress creates automatic excerpts from the post content – for archives, core/post-excerpt, feeds and REST – when a post has no manual excerpt (get_the_excerpt()). To do that, it renders only blocks that it knows contain text. Framework blocks tell WordPress which of their texts belong in an excerpt. excerpt: true on #[PlainText] or #[RichText] includes the value in automatic excerpts. It also works in list items, in value classes and with inspector: true. Blocks with such fields are added to excerpt_allowed_blocks. When WordPress renders a block for an excerpt, the block renders only its excerpt fields, one paragraph each: rich text as stored, plain text escaped. Neither render() nor the template runs. wp_trim_excerpt() then strips the tags. WordPress renders blocks for an excerpt while the get_the_excerpt filter runs, and offers no other signal. If other code renders blocks inside a get_the_excerpt filter, framework blocks render as excerpts there, too. WordPress never renders blocks with inner blocks for excerpts, so excerpt: true in such a block is a build error. For a container, use #[Block(excerptWrapper: true)] instead. It includes the excerpts of the container's allowed inner blocks, like core/group. Search Search is unchanged. WordPress searches the raw post content, and it finds single words of values in the block comment JSON, which stores non-ASCII characters as they are. It does not find phrases across formatting, nor values with &, <, > or " (stored as & etc.). Attribute names and enum values match, too. Attributes at render time WordPress validates the attributes against the schema before rendering: an invalid value falls back to the default. It does not sanitize them, though. The framework's value factory therefore sanitizes each attribute against its schema (rest_sanitize_value_from_schema()) and only then creates the attribute object. Attributes of block supports, WordPress' and your own, are not part of the attribute object. Errors An exception in render() or while the attribute object is created is rethrown if WP_DEBUG is enabled. Otherwise it is logged with error_log(), and the block renders nothing. The rest of the page still renders. Core blocks The framework disables no core blocks. Which ones a theme offers is the theme's decision. A hook on allowed_block_types_all limits them: final class AllowedBlocks { /** * @param bool|list $allowed * @return bool|list */ #[Hook('allowed_block_types_all')] public function filter(bool|array $allowed): bool|array { return ['core/post-content', 'core/template-part', 'sections/hero' /* … */]; } } Escaping Twig escapes every value unless you say otherwise. This table shows how each kind of value gets into the markup: Value Output #[PlainText] and other strings {{ attrs.topline }} – Twig's autoescaping #[RichText] {{ attrs.headline|raw }} – exactly as stored; WordPress filters it with wp_kses when a user without unfiltered_html saves #[Url] strings {{ button.url }} – the schema has format: uri, so the value is sanitized with sanitize_url() (disallowed protocols such as javascript: become empty) and then autoescaped Images #[Image] attachment ID with {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, size = 'full', attributes = {}) }} (wp_get_attachment_image(); empty for null; more in WordPress functions) References IDs; {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }}, {{ wp_post_url(attrs.target) }}, wp_term_name(), wp_term_url(), wp_user_name() and more WordPress functions (see References) Inner blocks {{ content|raw }} Root element {{ block_wrapper_attributes(extra = {}) }} (get_block_wrapper_attributes(): classes and anchor of the supports, plus the classes of block supports) Don't apply string filters such as upper to HTML: they change tags, URLs and entities too. Use CSS for uppercase text.
description: Blocks are the heart of a framework theme. Every block is rendered on the server from a Twig template, and content editors edit it inline in the editor canvas. This page shows how to write a block, which attributes it can have and how its values reach the markup.

title: Boot and modes
content:
Before the framework can register anything, your theme or plugin has to start it. That takes one call in the file WordPress loads first: functions.php for a theme, the main plugin file for a plugin. This page shows that call for each kind of project. It then explains the two modes the framework runs in: development mode for your checkout and release mode for production.

Boot

Themes

A theme loads Composer's autoloader and boots the framework in its functions.php:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Release builds ship prefixed dependencies in vendor-prefixed/; source checkouts use Composer's vendor/.
require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

Saij\WpAppFramework\Theme::boot();

The autoloader lines choose between two directories. In your Git checkout, Composer installs everything into vendor/. A release ZIP contains vendor-prefixed/ instead, with every dependency renamed into the theme's own namespace (see Release). If neither exists, require fails with a fatal error that names the missing path.

Plugins

A plugin does the same in its main file. The main file must be named after the plugin's directory, for example my-plugin/my-plugin.php, and it passes its own path to the boot:

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: My Plugin
 * Version: 1.0.0
 * Requires PHP: 8.5
 */

declare(strict_types=1);

require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

Saij\WpAppFramework\Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

The framework needs the file to find the plugin's directory and its URL; asset URLs of a plugin come from plugin_dir_url().

Child themes

A child theme without code needs neither a boot nor a build. It overrides templates of its parent theme and adjusts theme.json like any child theme.

A child theme with code of its own – blocks, hooks, REST routes – boots its own framework instance in its functions.php. It uses the same autoloader lines and Saij\WpAppFramework\ChildTheme::boot();. Child themes explains how it works next to its parent theme.

Slug and init action

Each instance is identified by a slug. For a theme it is get_template(), for a child theme get_stylesheet() and for a plugin its directory name. The framework derives every global name of the instance from it.

A slug can boot only once. A second boot with the same slug is an error, whether it comes from the same project or from a theme and a plugin that happen to share a directory name.

At the end of the boot the framework fires the action wp_app_framework/init/{slug}, without arguments.

The kind of project

The framework's build reads the kind of project from the type in its composer.json, which must be wordpress-theme or wordpress-plugin. A theme needs a style.css. If that file names a parent theme in its Template: header, the project is a child theme.

Modes

The framework reads your attributes in a build step and writes the result into a manifest (see Concepts). Where that manifest comes from depends on the mode, and the framework chooses the mode by itself. You never set a constant or a flag.

Release mode

A theme or plugin is in release mode when it contains generated/manifest.php. Only the release build creates that file, so release mode is what runs on a live site.

In release mode the framework loads the manifest as it is: no reflection, no file checks, and no writes into the theme or plugin directory. Compiled Twig templates go to a cache directory named after the template version of the release (see Twig templates).

Development mode

Without generated/manifest.php the framework is in development mode. This is the mode of your checkout. You change a class, reload the page, and the change is there.

The framework builds the manifest by reflection and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/, never in the project itself. To avoid rebuilding on every request, it works like Symfony's container cache in debug mode. A meta file records the files the build depended on, with relative paths only. On each request the framework compares modification times. Only for files that are newer does it recompute the class signature or the file content. The signature covers attributes, parents, interfaces, traits and the signatures of the constructor and public methods; it does not cover method bodies. Only a difference triggers a rebuild, so editing the body of a method costs nothing.

Several consumers in development mode

In development mode the framework and its dependencies are not prefixed. All consumers therefore share the same classes, and whichever autoloader runs first provides them. A plugin built against one framework checkout would silently run with the framework of the theme.

To rule that out, the boot checks two things and fails if either does not hold:

the loaded framework is the consumer's own vendor/saij/wp-app-framework, compared by real path;

the loaded Twig version is the one recorded in the consumer's vendor/composer/installed.php.

In practice, link the same framework checkout into every consumer. The option WP_PACKAGE_LINKS of wp-dev-env does exactly that.

description: Child themes are where customer projects adapt a theme: different markup for a block, adjusted colors, an extra block or two. The framework supports two kinds of child theme, and you pick the one that fits the job.

title: Editor
content:
Content editors should see a block in the editor exactly as it appears on the page, and type straight into it. Core blocks achieve that with an edit component in JavaScript, which duplicates the block's markup. A framework block has no such duplicate. Its markup exists only once, in the Twig template. This page explains how the editor runtime makes that work, how you mark editable elements in a template, what the generated inspector offers, and how to extend and build the editor scripts. How it works The framework ships an editor runtime, a script that your theme or plugin builds and the block editor loads. For each framework block in the editor it does three things: It asks the server to render the block, from the same Twig template the front end uses. It parses the returned HTML and finds the elements the template marked as editable. It replaces those elements with editors – rich text, an image picker, inner blocks – and keeps the rest of the markup as it is. The result looks like the front end because it is the front end's markup. When an editor changes a value in the inspector, the runtime renders the block again; when they type into a text field in the canvas, it doesn't, because the text is edited in place. Marking editable elements When the editor renders a block, the template functions field() and inner_blocks() mark the editable elements. On the front end they print nothing. Fields field(path) goes on the element that shows a field: {{ attrs.topline }}

{{ attrs.caption.text }} {% for button in attrs.buttons %} {{ button.label }} {% endfor %} The path names a #[PlainText], #[RichText] or #[Image] field of the block: a name, a dotted path into a value class, or a list with indexes for list items. Anything else throws an exception, in the editor and on the front end, so a typo never goes unnoticed. Text fields become WordPress' RichText with the element's tag. title: Hooks
content:
Hooks are how your code talks to WordPress. In a plain theme you would call add_filter() in functions.php, create the objects your callback needs, and count the arguments it accepts. With the framework, you put #[Hook] on a method instead. The build finds the method, and the framework registers the hook and creates the class only when WordPress actually fires it.

A first hook

This filter changes post titles with the help of a Formatter service:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Hook\Hook;

final class TitleFilter
{
    #[Hook('the_title', priority: 20)]
    public function filter(string $title, Formatter $formatter, int $postId = 0): string
    {
        return $formatter->format($title, $postId);
    }
}

Several things happen here without extra code:

Action or filter? The method returns a string, so the framework registers a filter. A method that returns void becomes an action.

Services in the signature. Formatter is a service (see Services), so the framework passes it in. You can ask for services in the constructor too; in the method signature they are handy when only this hook needs them.

WordPress arguments. All other parameters receive the arguments WordPress passes to the hook, in their order: $title gets the first, $postId the second. The framework derives accepted_args from them, so you never count by hand.

Optional arguments. If WordPress passes fewer arguments than the method declares, the missing ones use their default value. That is why $postId has = 0.

Several hooks on one method

#[Hook] is repeatable. The same method can listen to several hooks, each with its own priority:

#[Hook('the_title')]
#[Hook('single_post_title', priority: 5)]
public function filter(string $title): string { /* … */ }

When things go wrong

The class is created only when the hook fires for the first time, so a theme with many hooks loads only what a request uses.

If the method throws an exception, the outcome depends on WP_DEBUG. With WP_DEBUG enabled, the exception is rethrown and you see it right away. Without it, the exception is logged with error_log() and the site keeps running. A filter then returns the value it received, as if it had not run.

Rules

The method is public and non-static and declares a return type: void for an action, any other type for a filter.

Parameters typed with a service candidate are injected. All other parameters receive the WordPress arguments in their order; accepted_args is derived from them.

#[Hook(name, priority: 10)] is repeatable.

Services are created when the hook fires. Exceptions are rethrown with WP_DEBUG; otherwise they are logged with error_log(), and filters return their original value.

title: Plugins
description: A plugin uses the framework just like a theme. It boots its own instance with Plugin::boot(__FILE__) (see Boot and modes) and has its own blocks, hooks, REST routes, templates and settings. Everything in the guides applies to plugins as well. What is special about plugins is that they often work together with a theme. A plugin may provide data the theme displays, or helpers the theme's templates call. This page explains how a plugin – or a theme, towards its child theme – offers such an interface, and how the theme changes the plugin's markup.

title: REST routes
content:
A REST route in WordPress needs more code than it seems. You call register_rest_route(), write an args schema for validation, add a permission callback, read and convert the parameters, and turn errors into WP_Error objects with the right status code. Forgetting the permission callback makes the route public.

With the framework, a route is a method with #[RestRoute]. The framework derives the argument schema from the method signature, so WordPress validates and sanitizes the arguments before your code runs. The permission is a required argument of the attribute, so your IDE and the build report a route without one.

Controller and routes

Routes live in a controller class. #[RestController] on the class sets the REST namespace and an optional base path for all its routes:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\HttpMethod;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission\PublicAccess;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestController;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestException;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestRoute;

#[RestController('sections/v1', base: '/items')]
final class ItemController
{
    #[RestRoute('/{id}', HttpMethod::Get, new PublicAccess())]
    public function show(int $id, ItemRepository $items, Variant $variant = Variant::Short): array
    {
        return $items->find($id) ?? throw new RestException('sections_item_not_found', 'Item not found.', 404);
    }
}

This registers GET /wp-json/sections/v1/items/{id}. Read the method signature from left to right:

int $id matches the placeholder {id} in the path. Because it is an int, the route only matches digits.

ItemRepository $items is a service, so the framework injects it.

Variant $variant = Variant::Short is a backed enum with a default, so it becomes an optional request argument (?variant=long). WordPress accepts only the enum's values, and the method receives the enum case.

The method returns an array, which becomes a JSON response with status 200. If the item does not exist, it throws a RestException with status 404.

#[RestController(namespace, base: '')] takes the namespace without leading or trailing slash; the value may be a class constant. A #[RestRoute] in a class without #[RestController] is a build error.

#[RestRoute(path, methods, permission)] is repeatable, and all three arguments are required, so the IDE and the build both report a missing permission. path is empty or starts with /. methods is an HttpMethod case or a list of them.

Permission

Every route says who may call it. There are three kinds of permission, all in the namespace Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission:

new PublicAccess()                      // everybody
new Capability('delete_posts')          // current_user_can('delete_posts')
new Callback(self::canEdit(...))        // your own check

A callback decides with your own logic. It is a first-class callable of a public static method that returns bool. It must be static because PHP allows first-class callables in attribute arguments only for static methods.

#[RestRoute('/{id}', [HttpMethod::Put, HttpMethod::Patch], new Callback(self::canEdit(...)))]
public function update(int $id, string $title): WP_REST_Response { /* … */ }

public static function canEdit(int $id, ItemRepository $items): bool
{
    return current_user_can('edit_post', $items->getPostId($id));
}

The callback's parameters follow the same rules as those of the route: services are injected, and request arguments must exist in the route with the same name and type. Before calling it, the framework validates and sanitizes these arguments against the route's own schema and denies access if one is invalid. That matters because WordPress also calls permission callbacks to build the Allow header, with a request validated for a different route handler.

Path placeholders

{name} in the path matches the parameter with the same name. That parameter must be required and of type int (matches \d+), string ([^/]+) or a backed enum (its values). Its value always comes from the URL, never from a query argument with the same name.

Route paths may only contain letters, digits, ., _, ~, -, / and placeholders.

Parameters

The framework looks at each parameter of the method and decides where its value comes from:

A service candidate is injected.

WP_REST_Request receives the request itself.

Everything else is a request argument with the parameter's name: int, float, string, bool, a backed enum, or an array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] (see Values). Each may be nullable and have a default value.

A single value class without #[ListOf] is not supported as a request argument, because a parameter with a class type is treated as a service.

From the request arguments the framework builds the route's argument schema (type, enum, items, required, default). WordPress then does the work it always does with a schema: it validates and sanitizes the arguments, answers with 400 if one is invalid, and shows the schema on an OPTIONS request. Missing optional arguments get the parameter's default. Enums, value objects and lists are converted by the value factory, so your method receives typed values.

#[Param] (Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Param) adds further constraints to the schema:

public function update(
    int $id,
    #[Param(maxLength: 200)] string $title,
    #[Param(format: Format::Email)] ?string $contact = null,
): WP_REST_Response

Its arguments are description, minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, pattern and format (a case of Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Format). The build checks that each one applies to the parameter's type.

Responses and errors

What the method returns decides the response:

A void method responds with 204 No Content.

Any other value goes through rest_ensure_response() and responds with 200.

For another status code or extra headers, return a WP_REST_Response, e.g. new WP_REST_Response($data, 201).

#[RestRoute('/{id}', HttpMethod::Delete, new Capability('delete_posts'))]
public function delete(int $id): void
{
    // … responds with 204 No Content
}

For an error response, throw RestException(code, message, status, data) with a status between 400 and 599. Any other exception is an unexpected error. It is logged with error_log() and answered with status 500 and the code wp_app_framework_internal_error. Class, message, file, line and stack trace of the exception are included in the response only if WP_DEBUG is enabled, so a live site never shows its internals.

Like hooks, the controller and its services are created only when the route is called.

title: Services

toc.text: Only what is used is built

description: Most classes in a theme or plugin need other classes: a hook needs a formatter, a block needs the template renderer, a REST route needs a repository. You don't create these objects yourself, and you don't register them anywhere. You ask for them in the constructor, and the framework's container passes them in. TitleFilter asks for a Formatter, so the container creates one and passes it in. Formatter needs no registration: it is a class in the theme's src/, which makes it a service.

title: Settings
content:
Settings are values for the whole site that a theme or plugin makes configurable in the backend: a tagline, the logo, the page with the privacy policy, the default density of lists. You describe them as typed classes, as you do with block attributes. The framework takes care of the rest: it stores each group of settings in a WordPress option, it adds a settings page with a form for all groups, it passes the values to your services and templates as typed objects. Settings that several blocks share but that are stored per block, such as a color scheme for each block, are block supports, not settings. Declaring a group Settings come in groups. A group is a readonly class with #[SettingsGroup], and each setting is a public promoted constructor parameter with a default: use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Image; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Label; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Setting\SettingsGroup; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\ListOf; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Url; #[SettingsGroup('general', title: 'General', description: 'Shown on every page.')] final readonly class GeneralSettings { /** * @param list $links */ public function __construct( #[Label('Tagline')] public string $tagline = '', public Density $density = Density::Normal, #[Url] public string $contactUrl = '', #[ListOf(SocialLink::class)] public array $links = [], #[Image] public ?int $logo = null, ) {} } The settings page shows this group as a form: a text field for the tagline, a select for the density, a URL field, a list editor for the social links, and an image picker for the logo. #[SettingsGroup(name, title, description: '', position: 10)] takes these arguments: name consists of lowercase letters, digits and _ and starts with a letter. It is unique within the theme or plugin, and it names the option and the key in templates. title is the title of the group on the settings page. description is an optional text above its form. position orders the groups: lower values first, then by name. Every setting needs a default, because a setting is missing until the group has been saved for the first time. Types of settings Settings follow the rules of values: int, float, string, bool, backed enums, value classes and #[ListOf] lists, each optionally nullable. Enum cases are labeled with Labeled. #[Url] and #[Label] work as for block attributes, and #[Hidden] keeps a setting off the settings page. Some markers from blocks have a meaning in settings too: #[Image] on a ?int stores the ID of an attachment, chosen from the media library. It also works in value classes and list items. Print the image with wp_attachment_image(). A value class used both by a block and by a settings group edits its image in the block canvas there and in the form here. #[PlainText] is a text field. #[RichText(allowedFormats: null)] is edited with WordPress' classic editor, because the rich text of the block editor works only inside a block. allowedFormats may contain core/bold, core/italic, core/link, core/strikethrough, core/subscript and core/superscript; other formats are build errors. The editor keeps only these elements and line breaks, without paragraphs. Print rich text with |raw. When a user without unfiltered_html saves (for example on multisite), it is filtered with wp_kses_post(). References (#[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference]) are chosen with a search, one or as a list. Other markers do not fit: inspector and excerpt have no effect in settings. postContent is a build error. #[Content] marks the content of blocks and means nothing in settings. It is a build error, also in value classes that a group uses. A group class is not a service. It is created from the stored values, never autowired, and #[Hook] or other entry points on it are build errors. Storage Each group is stored in its own option, named {slug}_{name}, where {slug} is the slug of the theme or plugin with _ instead of -. The theme my-theme stores the group general in my_theme_general. The option holds an object with every setting of the group; settings missing from a saved object get their default. The framework registers the option with register_setting() on init, with its schema and show_in_rest. That makes it readable and writable through /wp/v2/settings under the same name. WordPress validates and sanitizes saved values against the schema there, and requires the capability manage_options for reading and saving. The option belongs to the theme's slug, not to the active stylesheet. A child theme without code therefore uses the settings of its parent theme, and switching to a child theme keeps them. A child theme with code and each plugin have their own groups and options. Using settings A service receives a group through its constructor: final class Footer { public function __construct(private readonly GeneralSettings $settings) {} #[Hook('wp_footer')] public function print(): void { printf('

%s

', esc_html($this->settings->tagline)); } } The group object is created from the stored values when it is first needed, and kept until the option changes. Groups can be injected into the constructors of services only, not as parameters of hooks, REST routes or template functions. Templates read the groups of their own theme or plugin through the global settings:

{{ settings.general.tagline }}

{{ wp_attachment_image(settings.general.logo, 'medium') }} settings exists only if the theme or plugin declares settings groups. An unknown group name is an error. Invalid stored values A stored value can stop matching its setting, for example when a case is removed from its enum. The framework replaces such a value with the setting's default and logs it (wp-app-framework: settings: … in the PHP error log). The other settings of the group keep their stored values, so one outdated value never resets the whole group. Settings page A theme or plugin with settings groups gets one settings page. Its title is the name of the theme or plugin: the Theme Name: header of style.css, or the Plugin Name: header of the plugin's main file. A missing name is a build error. Themes and child themes find the page under "Appearance", plugins under "Settings". Only users with manage_options can open it. Each group is a form built from the same controls as the block inspector: text, number, toggle, select, rich text, image from the media library, reference search, nested values and the list editor. Several groups appear as tabs; a tab with unsaved changes is marked with "•". One "Save" button saves all groups in a single request through /wp/v2/settings. If a value is invalid, WordPress rejects the whole request, the page names the group and the setting, and nothing is saved. The page script is built by the theme's or plugin's build, like the editor runtime (see Editor), to build/vendor/wp-app-framework/settings.js. Without it, the settings page fails with an exception naming the missing file.

title: Styles
description: Block markup is styled with Tailwind CSS 4. The work is split between the framework and the theme. The framework compiles the stylesheet and loads it on the front end and in the editor. The design – which Tailwind tokens exist and which WordPress values they point to – belongs to the theme. The framework ships no stylesheet for the front end of its own, because design tokens differ from theme to theme.

title: Block supports
content:
Some settings belong to many blocks at once. A color scheme is the typical example: a card, a section and a teaser should all offer the same choice, look the same in the inspector and produce the same class names. Copying an enum into every attribute class and a class into every template would work, but every new block would have to repeat it, and nothing would keep the copies in line.

A block support declares such a setting once. Every block that uses it gets an attribute, a control in the inspector and class names on its root element; the framework derives all of that in the build. WordPress uses the same idea for its own supports such as alignment, which you switch on with #[Supports].

Block supports apply only to the blocks of the same theme or plugin, not to core blocks or blocks of other instances. Values for the whole site rather than for a single block are settings.

Declaring a support

A support is a service class with #[BlockSupport] and a public method className(). The method receives the value of the attribute and returns the class names for it:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Support\BlockSupport;

#[BlockSupport('surface', label: 'Surface')]
final class Surface
{
    public function className(SurfaceTone $value = SurfaceTone::Light): ?string
    {
        return 'surface-' . $value->value;
    }
}

The signature of className() describes the whole support. Its parameter type sets the attribute's schema and the control in the inspector, and its default is the attribute's default. Here SurfaceTone is a backed enum, so the inspector shows a select, and blocks start with SurfaceTone::Light.

#[BlockSupport(attribute, label, group: SupportGroup::Styles)] takes three arguments:

attribute is the name of the block attribute, in camelCase (colorScheme). The names WordPress reserves (lock, metadata, className, anchor, align, style) and a name that another support of the same theme or plugin uses are build errors.

label labels the control.

group places the control in the "Styles" tab (SupportGroup::Styles) or in the block's "Settings" panel (SupportGroup::Settings).

className() has exactly one parameter, with a default. Its type is one of these, each optionally nullable:

Type	Control
backed enum	select; label the cases with Labeled
bool	toggle
int, float	number
string	text

Value classes and lists are not supported, and the parameter takes no attributes such as #[Label]. The method returns string or ?string: the class names for the value, several separated by spaces, or null or '' for none.

The class is a service. It can depend on other services through its constructor – for example to read the available color schemes from the settings – and it is created when a block with the support renders for the first time. A support that no block uses is not built.

Using a support

A block adds a support with #[UseSupport]. It is repeatable, one per support:

#[Block('sections/card', title: 'Card', category: BlockCategory::Design)]
#[UseSupport(Surface::class, default: SurfaceTone::Dark)]
final class Card
{
    public function render(CardAttributes $attrs): string { /* … */ }
}

The block now has the attribute surface. Its default comes from the parameter of className(); default overrides it for this block and must have the type of the value – a case of the enum, a bool, and so on.

The template doesn't need to know about the support. It prints the root element with block_wrapper_attributes(), as every block template does, and that adds the class names of all supports to the classes of WordPress' supports:

<article {{ block_wrapper_attributes({class: 'card'}) }}>…</article>

A block with supports that renders without calling block_wrapper_attributes() fails. That way a support never stays without effect unnoticed.

Like every attribute, the value is stored in the block comment, e.g. <!-- wp:sections/card {"surface":"light"} /-->. The attribute object passed to render() does not contain it; the support handles it.

The following are build errors: an attribute of a support with the name of a parameter of the block's attribute class, the same support used twice, and a class without #[BlockSupport] in #[UseSupport].

At render time

Before the block renders, the framework sanitizes the value against its schema, converts it to its PHP type (an enum case, for example) and calls className().

Each returned class name must consist of letters, digits, - and _, so it must equal its sanitize_html_class(). Anything else is an error, because a class name built from user data could otherwise break the markup. Errors are handled like the render errors of blocks: rethrown with WP_DEBUG, otherwise logged, and the block renders nothing.

Blocks rendered for an excerpt evaluate no supports.

In the editor

The control appears in the support's group, only in the default editing mode. In contentOnly mode – in patterns and template parts – it is hidden, as WordPress hides its own design settings there. Changing the value renders the block again, so the class names in the canvas come from the server, just like on the front end.

A script next to the support class can replace the generated control in every block that uses the support. For src/Support/Surface.php that is src/Support/Surface.editor.js; it is loaded with the runtime if a block uses the support:

registerSupportControl( 'surface', ( { value, onChange } ) => <SurfacePicker value={ value } onChange={ onChange } /> );

The component receives { value, onChange, attributes, setAttributes }. A control that a block registers with registerControl() for the same attribute wins over the support's control.

Styling

className() builds class names at run time, so Tailwind does not find them in the templates. Style them with CSS of the theme, or list them with @source inline(…) in src/styles.css (see Styles).
description: Some settings belong to many blocks at once. A color scheme is the typical example: a card, a section and a teaser should all offer the same choice, look the same in the inspector and produce the same class names. Copying an enum into every attribute class and a class into every template would work, but every new block would have to repeat it, and nothing would keep the copies in line. A block support declares such a setting once. Every block that uses it gets an attribute, a control in the inspector and class names on its root element; the framework derives all of that in the build. WordPress uses the same idea for its own supports such as alignment, which you switch on with #[Supports]. Block supports apply only to the blocks of the same theme or plugin, not to core blocks or blocks of other instances. Values for the whole site rather than for a single block are settings.

title: Twig templates
content: Markup in the framework lives in Twig templates, not in PHP strings. Twig escapes every value by default, so you don't have to remember esc_html() for each one; only |raw and functions marked HTML print a value unescaped. It also keeps markup readable, and it lets child themes and themes override the markup of a block without touching its code. Twig renders the markup of blocks and fragments your code produces, such as the body of a mail or an HTML response. Page layouts are not Twig; they are block templates and template parts, as in any block theme. Where templates live Templates sit in the src/ directory of the theme or plugin, next to the code that uses them (src/Hook/Mail.twig, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig), or in shared directories (src/Component/Button.twig). There is no separate views/ directory. A template name is always the full path relative to src/, including the extension: 'Component/Button.twig'. That holds in PHP and in templates alike. There are no relative names, so a name means the same thing wherever it appears. Rendering a template A service renders a template through the TemplateRenderer, which it asks for in its constructor. render(name, context) returns the HTML as a string: use Saij\WpAppFramework\Hook\Hook; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer; final class Mail { public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $renderer) { } #[Hook('sections_mail_body')] public function body(string $body, string $name): string { return $this->renderer->render('Hook/Mail.twig', ['body' => $body, 'name' => $name]); } } The Twig environment is created when the first template renders, so a request without templates pays nothing for it. Blocks render their templates the same way (see Blocks). Lookup A template name without a namespace is searched in several layers. The first layer that has the file wins: overrides/{theme-slug}/ of the active child theme, if it has that directory, the theme's src/, the framework's src/. A higher layer overrides a template by providing a file with the same path. For example, a child theme of my-theme changes the markup of the theme's hero block, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig, with its own overrides/my-theme/Block/Hero/Hero.twig. The theme's PHP code stays as it is. Sometimes you need exactly one layer, for example when an override extends the original template it replaces. @theme/… and @framework/… address exactly that layer and cannot be overridden: {% include 'Component/Button.twig' %} {# child overrides → theme → framework #} {% include '@framework/Component/Button.twig' %} {# exactly this layer #} wp-app-framework build lists the project's templates that override framework templates. Child themes and plugins The src/ of a child theme belongs to its own framework instance, if it boots one. Its templates are searched in its own src/, then in the framework's, and they never override templates of the theme. To override the theme, a child theme uses overrides/{theme-slug}/. A plugin's templates are searched in this order: overrides/{plugin-slug}/ of the child theme, overrides/{plugin-slug}/ of the theme, the plugin's src/, the framework's src/. A theme overrides src/Block/Note/Note.twig of the plugin my-plugin with overrides/my-plugin/Block/Note/Note.twig. Because overrides live in their own directory, the theme's templates in src/ never collide with the plugin's. @plugin/… addresses the plugin's own templates exactly. The plugin's Twig environment renders the override. The override therefore sees the plugin's template functions and filters and the context the plugin passes, not those of the theme. Compiled templates are named after the slug of their instance, so a theme and a plugin never share compiled code of templates with the same path. Environment Twig runs with settings that catch mistakes early: Autoescaping (html) is always on. strict_variables is always on, so an undefined variable is an error instead of an empty string. In development mode, debug, auto reload and dump() are enabled; in release mode they are off. A theme or plugin with settings groups has the global settings (see Settings). The framework provides the template functions of blocks (block_wrapper_attributes(), see Blocks), of the editor (field(), inner_blocks(), is_editor(), see Editor), has_plugin() (see Plugins) and the WordPress functions below. Twig exceptions reach the code that rendered the template, so the error handling of hooks and REST routes applies to them. Cache Compiled templates are cached in wp-content/cache/{slug}/twig/. Release mode compiles without auto reload: Twig never checks whether a template changed. Each release therefore uses its own directory, wp-content/cache/{slug}/twig/{templateVersion}/. The template version is a hash over the names and contents of all templates of the project and the framework; build --output writes it into the release manifest. Overrides add one more level. If the active theme or child theme overrides templates of another instance – a plugin, or the theme overridden by its child theme – that instance's cache directory gets a further level named after the versions of theme and child theme. A changed override therefore needs a new version of the theme or child theme. Directories of older releases are not removed yet. Template functions and filters Your own Twig functions and filters are methods of services with #[TemplateFunction] or #[TemplateFilter]: use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFilter; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFunction; final class Formatting { #[TemplateFunction('price')] public function price(int $cents): string { return number_format($cents / 100, 2, ',', '.') . ' €'; } #[TemplateFilter('highlight', html: true)] public function highlight(string $value): string { return '' . $value . ''; } } {{ price(total) }} {{ name|highlight }} The service is created when a template calls one of its functions for the first time. Like other services, it gets its dependencies through its constructor. Escaping By default Twig escapes the result of a function or filter. A method that returns HTML sets html: true; its result is printed as it is, and it must return string. An HTML filter receives the filtered value already HTML-escaped, unless the value is safe already (for example after |raw). Twig's nl2br works the same way. In the example, highlight can wrap $value in without escaping it first. Other arguments are passed unescaped: an HTML function or filter must escape every argument it puts into its result. Rules #[TemplateFunction(name, html: false)] and #[TemplateFilter(name, html: false)] go on public, non-static methods of services. Names are valid identifiers and unique per kind. They must not reuse a function or filter Twig provides, because Twig would silently replace it. Parameters must not be services (inject them through the constructor), variadic or by reference. A filter receives the filtered value as its first parameter. Callables offered to other consumers (public: true) are described in Plugins. WordPress functions Templates often need data from WordPress: an image for an attachment ID, the title and URL of a linked post, the site name. The framework provides these as template functions. Each is a thin wrapper around a WordPress function, and the wp_ prefix tells you so at a glance. {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }} {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, 'large', { class: 'rounded' }) }} {{ wp_post_date(attrs.target, 'j. F Y') }} The names follow one rule: wp_ + object + property, without get_ or the_. A WordPress function that already starts with wp_ keeps its name (wp_date, not wp_wp_date). The prefix is not reserved for the framework, but a name the framework already uses is a build error. The functions handle missing data for you: IDs may be null, for example an empty #[Image] or reference. null and objects that do not exist give '', so a template does not need to check first. Posts that are not publicly viewable count as missing, except when the block editor renders the block. Attachments are not checked for visibility. Text is escaped by Twig. Some values come from WordPress already escaped: term and user names, the site name and description, and the logout URL. The framework decodes them first, so they are not escaped twice. Functions marked HTML below print their result unescaped. Function WordPress Result wp_attachment_image(id, size = 'full', attributes = {}) wp_get_attachment_image() HTML wp_attachment_image_url(id, size = 'full') wp_get_attachment_image_url() URL wp_attachment_url(id) wp_get_attachment_url() URL wp_attachment_caption(id) wp_get_attachment_caption() HTML as stored (filtered with kses when saved without unfiltered_html) wp_attachment_alt(id) meta _wp_attachment_image_alt text wp_post_url(id) get_permalink() URL wp_post_title(id) post_title text wp_post_excerpt(id) get_the_excerpt() plain text: tags removed, entities decoded wp_post_date(id, format = '') get_the_date() text; '' uses the date format of the site wp_post_thumbnail(id, size = 'post-thumbnail', attributes = {}) get_the_post_thumbnail() HTML wp_term_url(id) get_term_link() URL wp_term_name(id) name of the term text wp_user_name(id) display_name of the user text wp_user_url(id) get_author_posts_url() URL of the author archive wp_avatar(id, size = 96) get_avatar() HTML; '' if avatars are turned off wp_home_url(path = '') home_url() URL wp_site_name() get_bloginfo('name') text wp_site_description() get_bloginfo('description') text wp_login_url(redirect = '') wp_login_url() URL wp_logout_url(redirect = '') wp_logout_url() URL with a nonce wp_is_user_logged_in() is_user_logged_in() true/false wp_date(format, timestamp = null) wp_date() text in the site's time zone and language; null for now wp_human_time_diff(from, to = 0) human_time_diff() text, e.g. "5 minutes"; 0 for now wp_number_format(number, decimals = 0) number_format_i18n() text wp_size_format(bytes, decimals = 0) size_format() text, e.g. "2 KB" The output of wp_logout_url(), wp_is_user_logged_in() and wp_avatar() depends on the request (a nonce, the login state), not only on the attributes of a block. Keep that in mind wherever output is cached.
