title: Values
content: Blocks, REST routes and settings all deal with structured values: a headline, a choice among variants, a list of buttons, a link to another page. In WordPress these arrive as untyped arrays, either from the block comment, the request or an option. The framework lets you describe them once, as typed PHP classes, and uses that description in two places: In the build, it derives a JSON schema from the class. WordPress uses the schema to validate block attributes, REST arguments and settings. At run time, the value factory turns the stored array into an instance of your class, with enums as enum cases and nested objects as objects. It does this without reflection. Block attribute classes, settings groups, nested value classes and #[ListOf] REST arguments all work this way, so what you learn here applies to all of them. Value classes A value class is a readonly class whose values are all public promoted constructor parameters: final readonly class Button { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $label, #[Url] public string $url = '', public ButtonStyle $style = ButtonStyle::Primary, ) {} } It declares no other properties. Elsewhere in the framework, class properties are never public; value classes are the exception, because they are plain data. Types A value can have one of these types, each optionally nullable: PHP type Schema int, float, string, bool integer, number, string, boolean backed enum the type of its values, with enum listing the case values value class object with properties array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] array with items A nullable type adds null to the schema type (type: [..., 'null']). PHP has no generic types, so a list says what it contains with #[ListOf]. Lists of scalars exist only for references. Enums and value classes must be in the scanned PSR-4 directories. A value class that contains itself, directly or indirectly, is a build error. Defaults and missing values The default value of a parameter becomes the schema's default: enums as their value, value objects as arrays. A missing value uses the constructor's default. Inside a nested value class, a parameter without a default is required in the schema. Unknown keys in nested objects are ignored, just as WordPress ignores unknown block attributes. Wrong values The value factory never coerces silently. A value that does not match its type throws an InvalidArgumentException that names the path to the value, for example buttons[1].url. Blocks, REST routes and settings each decide what happens next; see their pages. URLs #[Url] on a string adds format: uri to the schema, so the value is sanitized with sanitize_url(). Disallowed protocols such as javascript: become an empty string. References A block that links to another page, a setting that names the privacy policy page, a teaser that shows a category: these are references to WordPress objects. Storing the URL or the title would break as soon as someone renames the page. References store the ID instead, and the framework looks up the current data when it renders. #[PostReference(postTypes: null)], #[TermReference(taxonomies: null)] and #[UserReference] (namespace Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\) mark such IDs in block attributes, value classes and settings groups: #[PostReference(postTypes: ['page'])] public ?int $target = null, // one page, null without #[PostReference] public array $featured = [], // a list of post IDs, in order (list) #[TermReference(taxonomies: ['category'])] public ?int $topic = null, #[UserReference] public ?int $author = null, On ?int the parameter holds one reference, or null if nothing is chosen. On array it holds a list of IDs in the chosen order; there is no #[ListOf] for it. The schema is integer or ["integer", "null"], or an array of integers. postTypes and taxonomies limit the choice to these keys; null allows all viewable post types or taxonomies. The build does not check the keys against the registered types, because types are registered at run time. The search in the editor accepts only searchable post types and taxonomies. In blocks, a reference counts as content (role: content), like #[Image]. Editing References are edited with a search, in the block inspector and on the settings page. Posts and terms are searched through /wp/v2/search, which finds published posts only. Users are searched through /wp/v2/users; users without the capability list_users see only authors of published posts. A list shows its entries as cards that can be moved up, moved down and removed. Resolution Content changes after a reference was stored. A page is deleted, or put back into draft. The framework checks this when it creates the value. A reference becomes null, or is left out of a list, if its target: no longer exists, is of another type, or not of a viewable type, is a post that is not publicly viewable. A deleted page therefore simply disappears from the output; nothing is logged. Renders for the block editor keep posts that are not public, such as drafts, so editors still see what they chose. Output The WordPress functions take the IDs: wp_post_title(id), wp_post_url(id), wp_term_name(id), wp_term_url(id), wp_user_name(id) and more. They return '' for null and missing objects. Posts that are not publicly viewable count as missing outside the editor. {% if attrs.target %} {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }} {% endif %} Rules The following are build errors: a reference on a type other than ?int or array, or together with #[ListOf]; a reference combined with #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Content] or #[Url]; several references on one parameter; empty or invalid postTypes or taxonomies; a reference on a REST argument. Declare the ID as int there. Where values are used Blocks, REST routes and Settings describe what each of them adds to these rules.

title: wp-app-framework
content:
wp-app-framework is a PHP and JavaScript framework for building standalone full site editing themes, child themes and plugins for WordPress 7 on PHP 8.5. You write blocks, hooks, REST routes and settings as plain PHP classes with attributes. The framework turns them into everything WordPress expects: registered blocks with an attribute schema, an editor with inline editing, REST routes with validation, and a settings page.

The framework is a library, not a theme or a plugin. Your theme, child theme or plugin includes it through Composer; the documentation calls these projects consumers. The framework registers no blocks itself; the blocks, hooks and routes you see in WordPress come from your code.

Each consumer runs its own copy of the framework, called an instance. Everything with a global name – the REST route, script handles, the JavaScript global, the cache directory, the init action – is named after the consumer's slug (its directory name). That is why a theme and several plugins can run side by side, even with different framework versions. Concepts explains this and the other ideas the guides build on.

Principles

The framework follows a few rules that shape every part of its API. Knowing them makes many details in the guides easier to follow.

No markup in the post content. Every block renders on the server. The post content stores only a block comment with the attributes as JSON, for example <!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {"title":"Summer"} /-->; block supports are attributes too. You can change a block's markup at any time, and every post shows the new markup without being saved again. The one exception is a single #[RichText(postContent: true)] field per block, which keeps the text of paragraphs and headings in the post content (see Blocks).

Inline editing in the editor canvas. Content editors type directly into the block, as with core blocks. The markup still exists only once, in a Twig template: the editor renders the block on the server and replaces the marked elements with editors (see Editor).

Full site editing. Pages are made of block templates and template parts, as in any block theme. Twig renders the markup of blocks and fragments that your code produces, such as mails or HTML responses – never whole page layouts.

Plain WordPress. A release ships all dependencies, including the framework and Twig, prefixed with the consumer's own namespace. The server needs neither Composer nor Bedrock, and in a release two consumers never load each other's classes (see Release).

Compiled in the build, not at run time. A build step reads attributes such as #[Hook], #[RestRoute] and #[Block] and writes a manifest of plain data. Mistakes such as a missing permission or a service that cannot be created show up as build errors, and a release runs without reflection (see Boot and modes).

Status

The framework is in development (0.x). Minor versions may still contain breaking changes; Upgrading lists them and how to adapt your code.

These parts are ready to use:

the framework core: boot, service container, manifest build, development mode and #[Hook];

REST routes with #[RestController], #[RestRoute] and #[Param];

Twig templates with TemplateRenderer, #[TemplateFunction] and #[TemplateFilter];

server-side blocks with #[Block], #[Supports], typed attribute classes, #[ListOf] (also for REST arguments) and references to posts, terms and users;

block supports of your own with #[BlockSupport], #[UseSupport] and registerSupportControl();

settings with #[SettingsGroup], one option per group, a settings page, injection into services and the template global settings;

the editor runtime: inline editing in the canvas, a generated inspector, a batch render route and a webpack helper;

the release build wp-app-framework release (prefixed ZIP), release mode with a versioned Twig cache, and GitHub workflows;

plugins: Plugin::boot(), theme overrides of plugin templates, public APIs and public template callables;

child themes: ChildTheme::boot(), overrides of theme templates in overrides/{theme}/, public APIs and template callables of themes, and #[ThemeApi].

Where to start

If you are new to the framework, read Concepts first. Then follow Getting started, which sets up a theme with a first block. The guides then explain each part of the API in turn. Values describes the typed values that blocks, REST routes and settings share.

The test theme theme-dev-test contains a working example of every feature. It comes with the test plugin plugin-dev-test and the test child theme theme-dev-test-child. wp-dev-env provides a local WordPress for development.

Names

What	Name
Composer package	saij/wp-app-framework
PHP namespace	Saij\WpAppFramework
JavaScript import	@saij/wp-app-framework
JavaScript global at run time	window.wpAppFramework[slug], one per framework instance
Source code	github.com/saijsaij/wp-app-framework

title: Upgrading
content:
From 1.0 on, the consumer API only grows within a major version: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in behavior, and a theme built against 1.0 keeps working with 1.9. Before 1.0, a minor version may still break the API. This page lists every such change, why it was made, and what you need to change in your theme or plugin.

The documentation is published for each minor version. The version switcher in the navigation bar shows the documentation of other versions, so you can compare the old and the new state.

0.7

Template functions that wrap WordPress functions start with wp_. Before 0.7 a template could call post_title() or attachment_image(), and nothing showed that these were WordPress functions rather than framework functions or functions of the theme. 0.7 gives all of them the prefix wp_ and adds many more (see WordPress functions).

The old names are removed without aliases. A template that still uses one fails to compile with an unknown function, so you won't miss any. Rename them in your templates:

Before	Since 0.7
attachment_image()	wp_attachment_image()
post_url()	wp_post_url()
post_title()	wp_post_title()
term_url()	wp_term_url()
term_name()	wp_term_name()
user_name()	wp_user_name()

If your own template functions use one of the new wp_ names, rename them as well: a name the framework already uses is a build error.

0.3

Child themes override theme templates in overrides/{theme}/ instead of src/. Since 0.3 a child theme can have code of its own and boot its own framework instance with ChildTheme::boot() (see Child themes). Its src/ directory now belongs to that instance and can no longer hold overrides of the parent theme.

Move each override from the child theme's src/ to overrides/{theme}/, keeping the path. For the parent theme my-theme, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig becomes overrides/my-theme/Block/Hero/Hero.twig (see Twig templates).

0.2

The init action is named after the consumer. Since 0.2 plugins can use the framework next to a theme, and each runs its own instance. The single action wp_app_framework/init could not tell them apart, so it became wp_app_framework/init/{slug} (see Boot and modes).

Replace add_action('wp_app_framework/init', …) with the action of the instance you mean, for example wp_app_framework/init/my-theme.
